answer:
HYPOTHESIS (self-contained, data-grounded): Using the group-aggregate World Bank panel (1975–2015) for Sub-Saharan Africa (code "SSF" in the data; "SSA" in the metadata) and Lower-Middle-Income countries ("LMC", read here as the "developing countries" group), the effect of education expenditure on per-capita income is positive but modest and only partially robust for the developing/LMIC group, and cannot be reliably estimated for Sub-Saharan Africa. The education variable is "Adjusted savings: education expenditure, % of GNI" (the only education variable present, though the description calls it "government expenditure on education, % of total expenditure"), and the outcome is "GNI per capita, constant 2015 US$" (used as the proxy for the description's "per-capita GDP, 2010 US$").

For LMC over the full 1975–2015 window, a first-difference (growth-rate) regression with Newey–West HAC errors finds that a 1-percentage-point higher education-expenditure share is associated with about +1.6 percentage points higher annual growth in GNI per capita (coef +0.0164, p≈0.004, n=40); this effect, however, is NOT robust once the labor-force-participation control (available only 1991–2015) is added (coef +0.0189, p≈0.51), and in a log-level dynamic specification the education term is weak and insignificant (coef −0.058, p≈0.068 with labor; −0.018, p≈0.22 without). By contrast, Sub-Saharan Africa's per-capita GNI is available only for 2011–2015; in that short window education expenditure actually FELL (3.65%→3.15% of GNI) while GNI per capita ROSE (US$1,555→US$1,634), giving a strong negative co-movement (Pearson r≈−0.97; simple OLS slope≈−0.10, p≈0.007) that is not statistically reliable with only 5 observations and no room for controls.

Conclusion: the data do NOT support a uniformly larger positive effect of education spending on per-capita GDP in developing countries than in Sub-Saharan Africa. The developing (LMC) group shows a small positive, only partially robust growth association, whereas the Sub-Saharan Africa evidence is too limited (5 years) to estimate a reliable effect and, in the available window, points the opposite way (inverse co-movement). Caveats: (i) "developing countries" is interpreted as the LMC group; (ii) GNI per capita (constant 2015 US$) proxies for per-capita GDP (2010 US$); (iii) the education variable is adjusted-savings education expenditure as % of GNI, not % of total expenditure as described; (iv) the SSA code is "SSF" in the data vs "SSA" in the metadata; (v) results are group-level time-series associations, not causal country-level panel estimates, and endogeneity (reverse causality from income to education spending) plus autocorrelation limit causal interpretation (mitigated via a lagged education regressor, first-differences, and HAC standard errors).

payload.hypothesis: The effect of education expenditure (adjusted-savings education expenditure, % of GNI) on per-capita income (GNI per capita, constant 2015 US$, proxy for per-capita GDP) over 1975-2015 is positive but modest and only partially robust for developing (Lower-Middle-Income, 'LMC') countries, and cannot be reliably estimated for Sub-Saharan Africa ('SSF'). For LMC, a first-difference regression with HAC errors shows a 1pp higher education share is associated with ~+1.6pp higher annual GNI-per-capita growth (coef +0.0164, p=0.004, n=40), but the effect is not robust to adding the labor-force control (p=0.51) and is insignificant in a log-level dynamic spec. For SSA, per-capita GNI exists only for 2011-2015, where education share fell (3.65%->3.15%) while GNI rose (1555->1634 US$), a negative co-movement (r=-0.97) that is not reliable with n=5. Thus the data do not support a uniformly larger positive education effect in developing countries vs Sub-Saharan Africa: LMC shows a small positive, partially robust growth association; SSA evidence is too limited and points the opposite way. Caveats: 'developing'=LMC; GNI(const2015) proxies GDP(2010); education var is %GNI not %total-exp; SSA code is SSF not SSA; group-level associations, not causal country-level panel estimates (endogeneity/autocorrelation limit causal claims).
payload.workflow: 1) Parsed data/worldbank_education_gdp.csv (12 rows = 2 groups x 6 series; 41 year cols 1975-2015). 2) Reshaped long->wide panel (unit in {LMC,SSF} x year, log GNI per capita as outcome, education expenditure %GNI as regressor, enrollment/exports/labor as controls). 3) For LMC (n=41) estimated log-level dynamic (lagged DV + lagged edu) and first-difference specs with Newey-West HAC (4 lags), with and without the labor-force control (available 1991-2015). 4) For SSA computed the 2011-2015 (n=5) descriptive co-movement of edu spend and GNI per capita (correlation + simple OLS, flagged unreliable). 5) Compared LMC coefficient (direction/magnitude/significance) vs the SSA limitation and wrote the natural-language hypothesis. Code: analysis.py.
